html_en:
OpenAI is buzzing with quiet excitement, AI safety is getting a TypeScript makeover, and the industry is converging on a single uncomfortable truth: your evals are your product.

⚡ Something's Cooking at OpenAI

The most intriguing signal of the day came without a press release. @thsottiaux at OpenAI offered a tantalizing non-announcement:

"This might have been my best day so far at oai. Ridiculous amounts of fun and intensity. Future is bright." — @thsottiaux

A separate tweet hinted at collaborative workspaces coming directly to ChatGPT, with a colleague apparently shipping improvements daily. The vagueness is, of course, the point — but the energy reads as genuine. Something is close.

🔐 Agents Are Writing Code Faster Than We Can Review It — So Make the Compiler Do the Work

The most technically substantive contribution of the day came from Guillermo Rauch, who announced gdp-ts — a TypeScript library that forces AI agents (and humans) to prove they've performed authorization checks before calling sensitive functions, with the typechecker enforcing compliance at compile time.

"Agents are writing more code than we can review, and they thrive in tight loops with hard constraints that would frustrate us. We see this with the rise of Rust, borrow checker, code aesthetics debate and all." — @rauchg

It's a clever inversion: patterns from Haskell academia that were too cognitively expensive for humans become more valuable in an agentic world, precisely because agents don't get frustrated by rigid type systems. The library models a real Vercel constraint — changing a project password requires proving both role and entitlement. Ship bad auth logic and the build simply fails.

Meanwhile, @trq212 shared a complementary insight on agent efficiency: planning at a higher abstraction level is dramatically more token-efficient than generating raw HTML, because the model doesn't need to reconstruct common patterns like state machines or diagrams from scratch. The same builder also flagged a pattern worth watching — "local hands": Claude running in the cloud but accessing your local filesystem, hinting at deeper computer-use integrations ahead.

"my favorite name for this pattern is 'local hands', Claude runs in the cloud but can access your files locally — also coming to cowork" — @trq212

📊 Evals Aren't QA — They're the Spec

Two voices converged on a theme that will ring familiar to anyone who's shipped an agent in production. @realmadhuguru put it bluntly:

"The most common mistake teams make is to treat evals as an additional QA step once the agent is built. AI products are fundamentally different. Your evals are your product spec." — @realmadhuguru

Aaron Levie expanded the business case, arguing that enterprise agent adoption is bottlenecked not by model quality but by the absence of realistic test environments:

"It's impossible to know how agents are performing if you don't understand how well they're executing on your evals and how they'll perform in the future with a model change or workflow upgrade. Every enterprise has to do this 1 by 1 right now, which is obviously slow and tedious." — @levie

The upshot: eval infrastructure — simulated file systems, CRM environments, email sandboxes — is shaping up to be a serious enterprise category, not a footnote.

🌍 Language Learning Gets a Glow-Up (From Two Directions)

A delightful coincidence: two builders independently shipped language-learning tools on the same day, each with distinct aesthetics. @petergyang published a full tutorial on building a Japanese tutor powered by Gemini 2.5 Live voice APIs — complete with diorama-style art generated by Nano Banana. The goal is refreshingly human: learn 100 phrases before a trip.

Meanwhile, @ryolu_ — who writes beautifully about design and shipped a dual-subtitle Netflix extension with pronunciation guides for Japanese, Chinese, and Korean — offered a moving reflection on Steve Jobs and what it means to make things people love:

"We spend so much energy trying to beat humans. I wish we spent more time learning from people's lives and making them better." — @ryolu_

It's an oddly timely sentiment for an industry debating AGI timelines.

🔭 The Longer Arc: AGI Infrastructure and the Token Economy

Garry Tan sketched two intersecting thesis statements. First, on the coming era of AI-assisted science:

"AGI Science Loops are coming, and there will be Muse/Instinct for those AGI Science Loops. Halmos is building that." — @garrytan

Second, a more contrarian infrastructure point: lab-built harnesses have an incentive to maximize token consumption, which opens a real market for third-party harnesses that swap expensive token burn for deterministic, tested, repeatable code. Startups like Grep, he argues, can arbitrage this misalignment profitably.

Together, these threads point toward the same destination: the raw model layer is increasingly commoditized, and the value is migrating to whoever controls the scaffolding, the evals, and the constraints that keep agents from going off-rails. The compiler, it turns out, might be the most important AI product nobody's talking about.
html_zh:
今天的AI圈有一个清晰的主题：工具链正在成熟。从评估基础设施到代码安全约束，开发者们不再只是追问"AI能做什么"，而是开始认真思考"我们怎么让它做得又好又安全"。

🔥 OpenAI内部：有什么大事正在酝酿？

OpenAI研究员 @thsottiaux 今天发了一条让人浮想联翩的推文：

"这可能是我在 oai 迄今为止最棒的一天。荒谬地有趣，荒谬地紧张。未来一片光明。" — @thsottiaux

他没有透露细节，但随后提到同事 Sergio 正在 ChatGPT 中打造"协作空间"功能，并称其"每天都在突飞猛进"。配合他神秘地指向另一条推文说"真正的故事在这里"，可以合理推断：ChatGPT 即将获得某种多人协作或共享工作区能力。这与 Notion、Linear 等协作工具的赛道直接重叠，值得密切关注。

🛡️ AI写代码越来越多，谁来保证安全？

今天最有深度的技术讨论来自 Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch，他开源了一个名为 gdp-ts 的 TypeScript 库，核心思路是：在编译时用类型系统强制验证权限检查，让 AI agent 写出的代码在根源上就无法绕过安全边界。

"Agent 正在写出比我们能审查的更多的代码，而它们在有硬约束的紧密循环中表现出色——这些约束反而会让我们人类感到沮丧。我们从 Rust 的兴起、借用检查器以及代码美学辩论中都能看到这一点。" — @rauchg

这个观点很锐利：人类程序员觉得繁琐的强类型约束，对 AI agent 来说反而是优势。同样值得一提的是 @trq212 分享的"local hands"模式——Claude 运行在云端，但可以访问本地文件——并称其即将登陆协作工作区。另外他还指出，在游戏设计等场景中，让模型先做规划再生成内容，比直接输出 HTML 要节省大量 token。

📊 评估（Evals）：AI产品的真正核心

Box CEO Aaron Levie 和独立观察者 @realmadhuguru 今天不约而同地谈到了同一个问题：企业 agent 部署的最大瓶颈，是缺乏真实环境下的评估体系。

"最常见的错误是把 evals 当成 agent 构建完成后的额外 QA 步骤。AI 产品有本质上的不同——你的 evals 就是你的产品规格。" — @realmadhuguru
"如果不了解 agent 在 evals 上的执行情况，以及模型更换或工作流升级后的表现，就根本无法知道它们运行得好不好。每家企业现在都得单独做这件事，显然又慢又麻烦。" — @levie

Levie 直接点出这是一个巨大的市场机会：每家企业都将需要专人管理 evals、构建模拟环境。这与 Garry Tan 提到的 Grep 等创业公司的逻辑一致——实验室自己的工具链有烧 token 的动机，而第三方工具可以把 token 消耗转化为可复用的确定性代码。

🌍 构建者们在做什么：语言学习的两种路径

今天有趣的是，两位创作者几乎同时发布了语言学习相关工具，但路径截然不同。

@petergyang 用 Gemini Live API 构建了一个日语语音对话练习应用，并发布了完整教程，手把手教读者如何在出行前学会100个常用短语。Watch/Listen: 如何用 Gemini Live 构建 AI 语言学习应用

而设计师 @ryolu_ 则走了一条更安静的路：他做了一个 Chrome 插件，让用户在看 Netflix 时同时显示两种语言字幕，并附带日文、中文、韩文的发音指南。他今天还写了一篇感人至深的纪念 Steve Jobs 的文章，讲述自己如何从一台仿 Mac 的廉价 PC 出发，走上界面设计之路——读来令人动容，也让人不禁思考：在 AI 让技术越来越强大的今天，我们是否还在让产品变得更有人情味？

"我们花了大量精力试图超越人类。我希望我们能花更多时间去了解人们的生活，让它们变得更好。" — @ryolu_

⚡ 快讯

  • 美国开源模型追赶中： Replit CEO @amasad 认为美国在开源权重模型上正在追赶，同时他也为 Replit 上众多家庭式小企业用户感到自豪。
  • AGI科研循环： YC 掌门人 Garry Tan 点名初创公司 Halmos，称其正在为未来的 AGI 科学研究循环构建类似 Muse/Instinct 的基础设施。
  • 机器人学习： @adityaag 邀请 Berkeley 教授、机器人学习算法专家 Sergey Levine 参加 SPC 活动，探讨机器人如何从经验中学习。
